title: WannaCry — the $10 off switch that saved the hospitals

scenes.label: The day the screens turned red
scenes.narration: [dramatically] A 22-year-old stopped a global cyberattack with a $10.69 web address. [serious] It began on Friday, May 12, 2017. Hospital screens across England suddenly turned red. Patient files wouldn't open. A message demanded money. Soon, the same thing was happening around the world. The hero wasn't a cop or a spy. [softly] He was a surfer in a small beach town. But first, we have to go back two months.

data.label: the price of the off switch

visuals.at: a surfer in a small beach town

scenes.label: March: a fix nobody installed
scenes.narration: [calmly] In March 2017, Microsoft fixed a weak spot in Windows. Think of it as a new lock for a broken door. Britain's hospitals are run by the NHS, the country's free, government-run health service. It warned them to install the fix. But many computers never got it. Some still ran Windows XP, a version so old that Microsoft had stopped fixing it.

visuals.at: a new lock for a broken door

scenes.label: April: a spy tool gets loose
scenes.narration: [cautiously] Then, in April, a mystery group called the Shadow Brokers dumped hacking tools online. The tools were said to come from the NSA, America's biggest spy agency. One was called EternalBlue. It slipped in through that same weak spot. Now anyone could grab it. A few weeks later, someone did.

visuals.query: National Security Agency headquarters Fort Meade

scenes.label: Friday: WannaCry wakes up
scenes.narration: [serious] Then came Friday, May 12. The program was called WannaCry. It was ransomware. That's a program that locks your files and holds them hostage. To get them back, you had to pay $300 in bitcoin, a kind of digital money. And WannaCry had a nasty trick. It used EternalBlue to jump from computer to computer by itself. [ominously] Nobody had to click anything.

data.subject: Pay to get your files back

scenes.label: Hospitals in trouble
scenes.narration: [worried] By that afternoon, England's hospitals were in real trouble. Staff were locked out of their computers. Appointments were canceled. Five emergency rooms had to send ambulances elsewhere. In the end, at least 81 hospital groups were hit, plus nearly 600 family doctor offices. And the attack was still spreading.

scenes.label: Then the whole world
scenes.narration: [urgently] It wasn't just Britain. Spain's big phone company, Telefónica, told workers to shut down their computers. FedEx was hit. So were Renault car factories in France and Germany's national railway. Within two days, about 200,000 victims in 150 countries were counted. Phones, packages, cars, trains. Everything runs on computers. Who could stop it?

scenes.label: Meet the guy on his week off
scenes.narration: [warmly] Meet Marcus Hutchins. He was 22 and lived with his family in Ilfracombe, a seaside town in England. He loved to surf. He hunted bad software for a security company, working from his bedroom. That Friday was supposed to be his week off. He woke around 10 and went to lunch with a friend. [short pause] At about 2:30, he got home to news that the hospitals were under attack.

visuals.text: The NHS is under attack. - news that day

scenes.label: A strange web address
scenes.narration: [curious] Marcus got a copy of WannaCry and looked inside. He spotted something odd. Before doing any damage, it tried to visit a long, random web address. And nobody owned that address. So Marcus bought it for $10.69. It shows where an attack is spreading. [softly] As he said later, "The intent was to just monitor the spread."

visuals.text: The intent was to just monitor the spread. - Marcus Hutchins

scenes.label: The accidental off switch
scenes.narration: [surprised] The moment the address went live, it lit up. Thousands of infected computers were checking in every second. [pause] Every copy of WannaCry asked one question. Is this address out there? If no, it attacked. If yes, it stopped. [dramatically] Marcus had flipped an off switch by accident. In his words, "we actually stopped the spread just by registering the domain."

visuals.text: we actually stopped the spread - Marcus Hutchins

scenes.label: Too late for some, then a fight
scenes.narration: [sad] But the switch had a limit. It couldn't unlock computers already locked. Of 37 hospital groups fully locked out, 32 were hit before the switch. [serious] Then, on Saturday morning, someone aimed the Mirai botnet at the address. That's a huge army of hacked gadgets, like home cameras. [breathless] Marcus and his team kept it online. In two days, the switch prevented about a million infections.

scenes.label: A ransom that flopped
scenes.narration: [calmly] The ransom turned into a flop. Most victims didn't pay. By one early count, the attackers collected only about $55,000. No hospital group in England paid. Reporters soon found Marcus. He shrugged off the praise. [softly] "I'm definitely not a hero," he said.

visuals.text: I'm definitely not a hero. - Marcus Hutchins

scenes.label: From hero to handcuffs
scenes.narration: [serious] Three months later, in August 2017, Marcus flew to Las Vegas for a big hacker conference. As he headed home, the FBI arrested him at the airport. It wasn't about WannaCry. It was about a bank-stealing program called Kronos. Prosecutors said he helped make it years earlier, as a teenager. [slowly] The man who helped save the world now faced charges in America. So who built WannaCry?

scenes.label: The trail leads to North Korea
scenes.narration: [serious] In December 2017, the White House gave an answer. Tom Bossert, the president's homeland security adviser, said North Korea was responsible. He called the attack "cowardly, costly and careless." Britain agreed. In 2018, the Justice Department charged a North Korean programmer named Park Jin Hyok. Prosecutors said he worked for a front company tied to North Korea's military spies. He's still only accused.

visuals.text: cowardly, costly and careless - Tom Bossert

scenes.label: The bill, and the $10 hero
scenes.narration: [reflective] And Marcus? He pleaded guilty. In July 2019, a judge sentenced him to time served. No prison. WannaCry cost its health service about 92 million pounds and 19,000 canceled appointments. [long pause] [softly] The fix had been out for two months. In the end, a surfer, a weird web address and $10.69 saved the day. If you like true stories like this, subscribe to Breach Uncovered.

visuals.text: A $10.69 web address saved the day

facts.claim: WannaCry was released worldwide on Friday, May 12, 2017.
At least 81 of 236 NHS trusts in England were affected, plus 603 other organizations including 595 GP practices.
Five A&E departments had to divert patients.
All infected NHS organizations ran unpatched or unsupported Windows; NHS Digital issued alerts in March and April 2017.
Trusts were told in 2014 to have robust plans to move off Windows XP by April 2015.
Amyas Morse: the attack 'could have been prevented by the NHS following basic IT security best practice.'
32 of the 37 trusts locked out were in the North and Midlands & East regions, hit before the kill switch.
No NHS organization paid the ransom.
Roughly 200,000 victims in at least 150 countries within 48 hours; ransom $300 in bitcoin; 192 victims had paid 31.7 BTC (about $55,490).
Telefónica, FedEx, Deutsche Bahn, Renault, China National Petroleum Corporation and Iranian universities were affected; Wainwright quote.
WannaCry used EternalBlue, a leaked NSA tool released by the Shadow Brokers in early 2017.
Microsoft patched supported systems in March (MS17-010) and released an emergency XP patch on May 13, 2017; Brad Smith compared the leak to stolen Tomahawk missiles.
Hutchins registered the domain for $10.69; it registered thousands of connections per second; quotes on monitoring the spread.
Hutchins worked from his bedroom for Kryptos Logic; CEO Salim Neino said he 'not only saved the United States'.
Mirai botnet attacked the sinkhole the next morning; Hutchins awake 30+ hours; kill switch prevented about a million infections from triggering in two days.
Hutchins arrested August 2017 in Las Vegas over Kronos; sentenced July 26, 2019 to time served and one year supervised release by Judge Stadtmueller.
Bossert attributed WannaCry to North Korea: 'cowardly, costly and careless'; 'These disruptions put lives at risk'; UK's Ben Wallace 'as sure as possible'.
Park Jin Hyok charged in 2018; Chosun Expo front; damage 'hundreds of millions, if not billions'.
February 2021 indictment adds Jon Chang Hyok and Kim Il; RGB units known as Lazarus Group; Demers quote.
DHSC estimated WannaCry cost the NHS £92 million and 19,000 appointments.
Hutchins, 22, lives with his family in Ilfracombe, a seaside town in England, is an avid surfer, works from his bedroom; 'I'm definitely not a hero.'

On May 12 (his week off) Hutchins woke around 10 AM, went to lunch with a friend, returned home about 2:30 to news of NHS systems being hit, then registered the unregistered domain the sample queried.

Brad Smith (May 14, 2017): 'An equivalent scenario with conventional weapons would be the U.S. military having some of its Tomahawk missiles stolen'; governments should report vulnerabilities rather than stockpile them.
Shadow Brokers leaked EternalBlue in April 2017.

seo.youtube_title: How WannaCry Was Stopped: The $10 Web Address That Saved Hospitals
seo.youtube_description:
How was WannaCry stopped? The true story of the 2017 ransomware attack that froze hospitals in England, and the $10.69 web address that shut it down.
A WannaCry documentary: a leaked NSA hacking tool, a surfer working from his bedroom, and North Korea.

On Friday, May 12, 2017, a program called WannaCry started locking up computers and asking for $300 in bitcoin. It spread by itself from computer to computer, using EternalBlue, a hacking tool said to come from the NSA that leaked online a month earlier. In England, at least 81 hospital groups and nearly 600 family doctor offices were hit. Five emergency rooms had to send ambulances elsewhere. Within two days, about 200,000 victims in 150 countries were counted. Microsoft had released the fix two months before.

That afternoon, Marcus Hutchins, a 22-year-old in a seaside town in England, found a strange web address inside the code and bought it for $10.69. By accident, he had flipped WannaCry's off switch. Three months later, the FBI arrested him over different malware. The US and UK governments say North Korea was behind WannaCry, and the Justice Department has charged a North Korean programmer, who is still only accused.
